intro.html: These ten words are traps. Each one looks or sounds as if it means something it does not: enervate sounds like energize, noisome sounds like noisy, restive sounds like restful. Test writers love them for exactly that reason.

The rule for this topic: never trust the sound. Enervate = weaken. Nonplussed and bemused = puzzled. Noisome = smelly. Restive = restless. Peruse = read closely. Belie = give a false picture of. Sanction and cleave each have two opposite meanings. Inflammable = burns easily.
When one of these words appears in a reading passage, slow down and let the sentence around it tell you which meaning fits.

words.def: to weaken; to drain of energy
words.ex: The long, humid afternoon {enervated} the hikers, and they barely made it back to camp.
words.ctx: Far from energizing the team, the three-hour meeting {enervated} everyone; by the end, even the coach was slumped in his chair, too tired to speak.

roots.means: to make, to act on (in verbs)

words.etym: From Latin enervare, “to cut out the sinews”: e- (out) + nervus (sinew).
words.note: Enervate means nearly the opposite of energize, though the two look alike.

mn.text: The heat wave drains every bit of nerve and strength out of Sven; he flops on the sand like a wet noodle. The heat {enervates} him.

scene.alt: A big man slumps on the hot sand, drained of energy, beside a nearly empty battery.

words.def: so puzzled that one does not know what to say or do
words.ex: When the parrot answered the phone, the caller was completely {nonplussed}.
words.ctx: The magician’s final trick left the audience {nonplussed}; no one could explain how the elephant had vanished from the stage, and for a moment nobody even clapped.
words.etym: From Latin non plus, “no more”: a point at which nothing more can be said or done.
words.note: In careful writing, nonplussed means puzzled. A newer, informal American use means unbothered, nearly the opposite, so read it with care and use it for puzzled.

mn.text: Ms. Ada asks Kai, “What is forever plus one?” He opens his mouth, closes it, and just stares, with nothing more to say. He is {nonplussed}.

scene.alt: A teacher asks a tricky question and a boy stares back, too puzzled to answer.

words.ex: The tourists looked {bemused} by the street signs written in three languages.
words.ctx: Kai stared at the rules for the new board game, {bemused} by all forty of them, and finally went back to his book.
words.note: Bemused means puzzled, not amused. Some writers now use it for a puzzled sort of amusement, which is why careful readers check the context.

mn.text: Uncle Sven turns the new remote over and over, staring at its forty buttons; he is not amused, just confused: {bemused}.

scene.alt: A man stares, puzzled, at a remote control covered in buttons.

words.def: having a very bad smell; also, harmful
words.ex: A {noisome} odor drifted from the lunch box forgotten at the back of the closet.
words.ctx: Despite what its name suggests, the swamp was not noisy at all; it was {noisome}, giving off a stench of rotting plants that made visitors hold their noses.
words.etym: From Middle English noy (annoyance) + -some. It has nothing to do with noise.
words.note: Noisome means smelly or harmful, not noisy.

mn.text: The tuna sandwich forgotten in Dev’s gym bag for a week smells so bad that the whole team holds its nose; the bag is {noisome}.

scene.alt: Two teens recoil from a gym bag giving off a terrible smell.

words.ex: The {restive} horse stamped and tossed its head at the starting gate.
words.ctx: After two hours of waiting in the heat with no explanation, the crowd grew {restive}, shouting and pushing toward the locked gates.
words.etym: From Anglo-French restif, “balky, refusing to move,” from rester (to stay, to resist).

mn.text: Told to wait at the gate, the young horse stamps, snorts and tosses its head; it is anything but restful. It is {restive}.

scene.alt: A restless horse rears and stamps near a gate while its owner tries to calm it.

words.def: to read carefully; also, often, to look over casually
words.ex: Before signing, Dad {perused} every page of the lease.
words.ctx: Rather than skim the contract, the lawyer {perused} it line by line, circling three clauses that would have cost her client thousands of dollars.
words.note: Careful writers use peruse for reading closely, but many people now use it to mean browse or glance over. On a test, choose the careful sense unless the sentence clearly says otherwise.

mn.text: Professor Edwin reads the old treasure map with a magnifying glass, every tiny word and line, twice; he {peruses} it.

scene.alt: An old professor studies a map closely through a magnifying glass.

words.def: to give a false picture of; also, to show to be false
words.ex: Her calm smile {belied} how nervous she felt before the recital.
words.ctx: The tiny restaurant’s plain front {belies} the feast inside; customers who wander in expecting a quick snack find a seven-course dinner waiting.
words.etym: From Old English beleogan, “to deceive by lying”: be- + leogan (to lie).
words.note: Belie has nothing to do with believe: if her smile belies her fear, the smile hides it.

mn.cue: BE-LIE: the LOOKS tell a LIE
mn.text: Grandma’s rusty little car looks as if it could barely roll, but at the go-kart track it zooms past everyone; its shabby looks {belie} its speed.

labels.text: BE-LIE: the LOOKS tell a LIE

scene.alt: A rusty little car zooms past at top speed while its grandmother driver cheers.

words.def: official approval; also, a penalty for breaking a rule
words.ex: The club cannot hold its bake sale without the principal’s {sanction}.
words.ctx: The league imposed a harsh {sanction} on the team for cheating: it was banned from the playoffs and had to give back its trophy.
words.etym: From Latin sanctio, “a decree, a binding law,” from sancire (to make sacred, to decree).
words.note: Sanction can mean two nearly opposite things: approval (the school’s sanction) or a penalty (sanctions against a country). The verb to sanction usually means to approve. Let the sentence tell you which.

mn.cue: SANCTION: an OK... or a PENALTY
mn.text: Judge Edwin stamps OK on the parade plan, a {sanction} that lets it go ahead; then he fines the band that marched through the flower beds, a sanction of the other kind.

labels.text: SANCTION: an OK... or a PENALTY

scene.alt: A judge with a gavel stands between a sign reading approved and a sign announcing a fine.

words.def: to split apart; also, to cling closely
words.ex: With one swing of the axe, Grandpa {cleaved} the log in two.
words.ctx: The bitter argument {cleaved} the club into two camps, and for months the members sat on opposite sides of the room.
words.etym: Two Old English verbs fell together into one: cleofan (to split) and clifian (to stick, to cling).
words.note: Cleave is its own opposite: to split apart, or to cling together (“the child cleaved to her mother”).

mn.cue: a CLEAVER SPLITS... a sloth CLINGS
mn.text: Grandpa’s axe splits the log in two, while in the tree above, a sloth clings tight to its branch; to {cleave} can mean either one.

scene.alt: A grandfather splits a log with an axe while a sloth clings to a branch above.

words.def: easily set on fire; the same as flammable
words.ex: Keep the {inflammable} paint thinner far away from the stove.
words.ctx: Many people think the in- on the warning label means “not,” but the barrels marked {inflammable} were dangerous: a single spark could set them ablaze.
words.etym: From Latin inflammare, “to set on fire”: in- (into) + flamma (flame).
words.note: Inflammable and flammable mean the same thing. Because people mistook the in- for “not,” safety labels now usually say flammable.

mn.cue: IN-FLAME-able: can go up IN FLAMES
mn.text: One spark could send the barrel up in flames, so Marcus keeps the torch far away; the barrel is {inflammable}: it burns easily.

scene.alt: A worker in a hard hat holds up his hands to keep a burning torch away from a barrel marked with a fire warning.

head: word
sounds like it means
really means
after.cap: Ten traps: what each word seems to mean, and what it does mean.

after.html: Sanction and cleave are called contronyms: words that are their own opposites. Only the sentence can tell you which meaning the writer wants.

items.q: True or false: an enervating day leaves you full of energy.
items.why: False. To enervate is to weaken or drain. An enervating day leaves you exhausted.

items.q: A noisome swamp is one that is…
items.why: Noisome means foul-smelling or harmful; it has nothing to do with noise.

items.q: “The restive crowd pushed against the gates.” The crowd was…
items.why: Restive means restless and hard to control, not restful.

items.q: True or false: a barrel labeled inflammable is safe near a flame.
items.why: False. Inflammable means the same as flammable: it catches fire easily. The in- means into, not not.

items.q: In careful writing, a nonplussed person is…
choices: so puzzled he does not know what to say
items.why: Nonplussed traditionally means puzzled, at a loss. The newer “unbothered” use is informal and often seen as an error.
